title: Cognitive Biases in UX Research
intro: Calabro's guide started as a reference for one UX team. It gives each of 20 biases a definition, an example and an antidote, so a team shares vocabulary. Read the group that matches where you are in the work.

learn.title: Group 1: Study design (10)
learn.text:
These creep in when you design a study or write a task.

**Framing effect:** how you ask shapes the answer.
**Serial-position effect:** first and last list items seem more valuable.
**Self-reporting bias:** reported values differ from actual ones.
**Base-rate neglect:** misreading what small samples do to percentages.
**Power-user fallacy:** assuming frequent users behave drastically differently.

try.q: You open a task with “Others found this difficult, so take your time.” Which bias did you introduce?
try.explain: The set-up shapes the response. Write neutral task introductions.

learn.title: Group 2: Interpretation (7)
learn.text:
These come from inside our own heads during synthesis.

**Confirmation bias:** only looking for evidence that supports your hypothesis.
**Hindsight bias:** retrofitting logic onto past actions.
**Sunk cost fallacy:** the more invested, the harder to abandon.
**Motivated reasoning:** arguments for what we want to believe feel stronger.
**Recency bias:** newer information seems more accurate.

try.q: After six months on a feature, the team keeps arguing against test results that say users don't need it. Which bias fits best?
try.explain: The more time invested, the harder it is to let go.

learn.title: Group 3: Judging users (3) and pile-ups
learn.text:
**Implicit bias:** automatic associations that affect judgment.
**Attribution error:** over-crediting personality, under-crediting context.
**False consensus effect:** believing others think and speak like we do.

Biases stack. Dismissing a finding because “it came from a new user” can combine the power-user fallacy, myside bias and attribution error at once.

try.q: “That participant just wasn't very technical.” Which bias is most likely at work?
try.explain: It blames the person and ignores the context: the design.

test.q: How is each bias presented in Calabro's guide?
options: Name, severity score, owner, due date
test.explain: Three parts, so it works as a quick reference.

test.q: What is the main purpose of the guide?
options: Replace the need for usability tests
test.explain: Spotting and naming a bias gives you the power to manage it.

test.q: Which bias is in the “study design” group?
test.explain: It affects how lists and stimuli are presented, so randomise and rotate.

test.q: You are about to synthesise interview data. Which group should you re-read?
test.explain: Confirmation bias, sunk cost and motivated reasoning show up during synthesis.

test.q: What is “bias bias” in his list?
options: Experts trusting complex explanations over simple ones
Seeing bias in every research finding that you happen to dislike
Blaming users for the team's mistakes
Preferring recent data to older data
test.explain: It is one of the ten study-design biases.
